items.title: Plans for a new marine protected area boost whale shark conservation in Indonesia’s Saleh Bay
items.summary: Plans to create a marine protected area for whale sharks in Indonesia’s Saleh Bay would give the world’s largest fish important new protections across several stages of its lifecycle, conservationists say. Besides serving as a migratory route and feeding ground for adults, there is growing evidence that the sheltered bay acts as a safe haven for juvenile whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), allowing them to develop in waters rich in food but free of predators. Sightings of newborns also indicate the bay may be a whale shark pupping ground, which would make it the first-ever to be documented anywhere in the world, although researchers caution this is yet to be confirmed. According to a document from the provincial government, seen by Mongabay, the marine protected area (MPA) would cover 90% of known whale shark hotspots in Saleh Bay, which lies in the shadow of the volcanic Mount Tambora on Sumbawa Island in West Nusa Tenggara province. The species, classified as endangered by the IUCN, has been monitored there since 2015. The MPA has received the support of the West Nusa Tenggara provincial government and local communities, with conservationists now waiting on a final decision from Jakarta. A whale shark in Saleh Bay, 2016. Besides serving as a migratory route and feeding ground for adults, there is growing evidence that the sheltered bay acts as a safe haven for juvenile whale sharks. Image by Egaryan Saadi via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). “[The MPA] is important because this bay represents a key…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Plans for a new marine protected area boost whale shark conservation in Indonesia’s Saleh Bay

items.title: Singapore investors hope for diplomatic help after Indonesia halts $50b electricity export push
items.summary: SINGAPORE — With Singapore’s appetite for electricity expected to balloon by as much as half its current peak demand by 2031, the country is turning to its neighbors to pipe in clean power — in part to keep its data centers humming and support the uptake of electric vehicles. The city-state, which has little room to spare for large-scale power generators of virtually any type, has inked agreements to import electricity from Indonesia, Malaysia and Vietnam, and even as far afield as Australia. Singapore aims to reach net-zero carbon emissions by the middle of the century. In early 2025, the government said it would reduce the contribution of gas to its power-generating mix to 50% by 2035 — down from 95% currently. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority has granted conditional approval to several companies, most recently in 2024, to import a total of 3.4 gigawatts of low-carbon electricity from Indonesia by the middle of the next decade, a quarter of what Singapore estimates it will need by then. Now, those plans hang in the balance after Indonesia said it will not allow them to go ahead. There appears to be an intensifying diplomatic standoff, in part, over haze and energy. Singapore has let its frustration with the transboundary haze from its larger neighbor known. In late October, National Environment Agency publicly called on 10 Singapore-based plantation companies to take action regarding possible fires on their Indonesian concessions. The move came just over a week after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong indicated the…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Singapore investors hope for diplomatic help after Indonesia halts $50b electricity export push

items.title: Thailand-Myanmar river pollution agreement was weakened, then signed. China remains silent
items.summary: MAE SAI, Thailand — Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow made a one-day visit to Naypyidaw, the capital of Myanmar, on Nov. 12 to speak with the military regime about trade, border security and, notably, the pollution of Thai rivers that have been contaminated by mining pollution. While Thailand’s foreign ministry reported that transboundary pollution flowing from mines in Myanmar through rivers into Thailand was discussed, the visit underscored the lack of progress on bilateral solutions to the heavy metal contamination that has afflicted multiple rivers across northern Thailand since early 2025. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ press release noted that both the Thai and Myanmar representatives agreed to convene a joint working group on the issue “as soon as possible” and that a joint field visit would follow. Sihasak’s visit comes three months after Myanmar and Thailand signed a six-page agreement laying out the terms to jointly monitor the ongoing transboundary water pollution crisis linked to unregulated mining operations in Myanmar. Sources within the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed to Mongabay that the joint working group born out of this agreement has not met once since the agreement was signed Aug. 6. Even before the delay, the agreement on river pollution monitoring was met with sharp criticism by civil society and government officials who warned that the numerous revisions to the agreement — requested by the Myanmar side and accepted by the Thai side — meant that the bilateral efforts would likely fail to achieve anything meaningful for the…
items.t: Thailand-Myanmar river pollution agreement was weakened, then signed. China remains silent

items.title: Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting
items.summary:
Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast

Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.

The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

Continue reading...
items.t: Band of baby sea turtles swims out to sea after historic California nesting

items.title: Fish pay the price for sacred rituals at Mumbai’s Banganga Tank
items.summary: In October, hundreds of fish were found dead in Mumbai’s Banganga Tank, an ancient freshwater tank considered sacred with roots in Indian mythology. Fish deaths have become nearly an annual occurrence there following the Pitru Paksha rituals, when flowers and various food items are immersed in the water. The immersions likely cause a severe drop in dissolved oxygen levels, killing aquatic life in the tank, experts say. “This has been going on for the last 10 years,” activist Rohit Manohar Joshi, president of Yeoor Environmental Society, told Mongabay. “Every year, fish die because of the rituals performed during Pitru Paksha.” Banganga Tank is a 10-meter- (33-foot-) deep water tank located within the expansive Walkeshwar Temple complex. The water in Banganga Tank is fed by a natural underground freshwater spring below the tank on Mumbai’s Malabar Hill. Every year, several Hindu devotees observe Pitru Paksha during a 15-day period in September-October, when they perform rituals to honor their ancestors. During these rituals, they also immerse flowers and food items, including rice, flour and ghee, into the tank. Media reports have documented fish deaths following the ritual immersions as far back as 2014. In 2025, the city’s municipal corporation (BMC) reportedly removed 10,000 kilograms (22,000 pounds) of dead fish and floral waste. Last year, activists had written to officials seeking the provision of artificial immersion tanks, similar to those set up near beaches during the Ganpati festival, where devotees could immerse their offerings instead of directly polluting the…
items.t: Fish pay the price for sacred rituals at Mumbai’s Banganga Tank

items.title: Pataxó Indigenous people protest the arrest of a female vice-chief in Brazil’s Bahia
items.summary: Pataxó Indigenous people occupied the entrance to the Civil Police station in the city of Eunápolis, in the far south of Brazil’s Bahia state on Nov 12. It was a peaceful protest against the arrest of two Pataxó leaders in the Barra Velha Indigenous Territory. Erilsa Braz dos Santos, known as Uruba Pataxó, vice-chief of Barra Velha Mother Village, and communicator Karen Pataxó were arrested on Nov. 11 on suspicion of drug trafficking in the region. The Pataxó deny the accusations. Karen was released, but Uruba remained in custody and was transferred to a prison in the city of Teixeira de Freitas on Nov. 12, sparking outrage and mobilization among Indigenous people on social media. “This is a political accusation, because she is a leader who defends her people and her territory,” a protester said in a video published on Instagram by the Media and Art Research Center (Nupomar) and Barra Velha Village during the Eunápolis demonstration. Uruba and Karen were detained during Operation Barra Velha, carried out by the Civil and Military Police in Bahia’s Porto Seguro municipality. According to Indigenous leader Dário Pataxó, the imprisonment is intended to silence those who speak out against drug trafficking in the territory. “We know that their intention is to stop the movement. Uruba is one of those on the frontline. They’ve already stopped [Cacique] Suruí, who was president of the Barra Velha Council of Chiefs and is facing proceedings under house arrest. And now they want to stop Uruba,” Dario told…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Pataxó Indigenous people protest the arrest of a female vice-chief in Brazil’s Bahia

items.title: Environmental groups challenge Mexico’s rollback of protections for world’s smallest porpoise
items.summary: MEXICO CITY — Environmental groups are fighting against relaxed fishing regulations in the Gulf of California, where the last of the vaquita, the world’s smallest porpoise, is close to extinction. In October 2026, changes to the regulations dramatically reduced the area where fishing is prohibited in vaquita habitat. In response, several environmental groups have asked a court to halt the changes, arguing that they threaten the last approximately 10 vaquitas (Phocoena sinus) remaining in the world. “The court can stop this rollback before more of the habitat is exposed to deadly nets,” said Aleira Lara Galicia, executive director of Greenpeace Mexico, one of the groups that filed the Nov. 6 injunction request. The Center for Biological Diversity and the Conservation of Marine Mammals of Mexico were also listed as petitioners. The vaquita averages around 1.5 meters (5 feet) long and weighs up to 54 kilograms (120 pounds). It’s endemic to the Gulf of California, also called the Sea of Cortez, where illegal fishing has decimated vaquita populations over the last three decades. The decline is primarily the result of bycatch in gillnets, which hang down vertically in the water and can drown a vaquita when it gets entangled. Many gillnets are illegally set for totoaba (Totoaba macdonaldi), an endangered fish with a swim bladder that sells for thousands of dollars on the black market, primarily in Asia. To protect the vaquita and other marine life, the gulf has a series of layered and overlapping protected areas. A 225-kilometers squared (approximately…This article was…
items.t: Environmental groups challenge Mexico’s rollback of protections for world’s smallest porpoise

items.title: The power of the paddy: Japan looks to rice fields to help mitigate flooding
items.summary: OSAKI, Japan — Osaki, an agricultural community in northeast Japan, has struggled with flooding in recent years. The area was inundated in 2015, 2019 and 2022, when heavy rains breached river embankments. In response, Osaki farmers and local government have installed more than 5,000 small, earthen dams in the rice paddies that surround the community, according to city officials. They say they hope the dams will mitigate flooding by keeping more water contained to the fields. Speaking to Mongabay, Osaki city officials attribute the uptick in floods, in part, to climate change. It’s a pattern seen across Japan, where climate change-fueled heavy rainfall events have increased in frequency and intensity, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. In response, officials are rethinking their approach to flood control, with increased focus on “green infrastructure” solutions in rice paddies and other agricultural areas. Japan’s agricultural sector is in decline: The average age of a farmer was nearly 70 in 2026 and the country’s rural population is on a steady downward trend. Agricultural land near cities has been converted into suburbs and industrial zones; these low-lying urban areas can be particularly vulnerable to flooding. With declining agricultural land in mind, researchers have been assessing the flood mitigation potential of not only current agricultural land but also abandoned fields. They say that these assessments highlight the importance of understanding site-specific conditions and developing local countermeasures against flooding. “We need to look at the value…
items.t: The power of the paddy: Japan looks to rice fields to help mitigate flooding

items.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and crucial this issue is for the Sámi culture,” Inger-Ann Omma, a lawyer and reindeer owner from the Vapsten Sámi village reindeer herding district, tells Mongabay. Sweden’s environmental protection agency says it is implementing methods to fix parts of the system. For 30 years, the Swedish government has operated one of the world’s longest running Conservation Performance Payment (CPP) programs of its kind. Rather than compensating reindeer herders for individual reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) losses, this system rewards the Sámi reindeer herding communities based on the presence and reproduction of large carnivores, such as wolverines (Gulo gulo), lynx (Lynx lynx) and wolves (Canis lupus). Reindeer herding is a central part of traditional Sámi culture and livelihood — approximately 13,000 people practice it today in the Sámi homelands of Sweden, Norway and Finland. Reindeer are semi-domesticated animals that spend a lot of their time unsupervised, leaving them vulnerable to carnivores. As many as 50,000 to 100,000 reindeer are estimated to be killed each year by these carnivores in the Fennoscandian region across Northern Europe, putting financial burden onto the reindeer…
items.t: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders

items.title: Pope in Peruvian rainforest demands justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting Amazon
items.summary: PUCALLPA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is demanding justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon. During a visit deep in the Peruvian rainforest, Leo fully backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal exploitation. Leo was channeling one of Pope Francis’ core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation. He said “The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable.” Leo spoke to Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the northeastern city of Pucallpa. By  Nicole Winfield, Astrid Suarez and Mauricio Savarese,  Associated Press Banner image: Children present an offering to Pope Leo XIV outside the cathedral in Cusco, Peru, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Image courtesy of Jose Sotomayor, Associated PressThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Pope in Peruvian rainforest demands justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting Amazon

items.title: Drowned in fishing gear, struck by boats, North Atlantic right whales in serious trouble
items.summary: North Atlantic right whales hover near extinction, with perhaps 382 remaining, according to a new census published today. Their numbers dropped from 389 in 2024, a 1.8% decline, though the number of female right whales of reproductive age has remained steady at 73. The survey was conducted and published by scientists at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life, based in Massachusetts, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the U.S. federal regulatory agency. North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) are among the world’s most endangered marine mammals, listed as critically endangered by IUCN, the global conservation authority. These numbers were released at the start of the annual meeting of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium, a collaboration that includes researchers, conservationists, shipping and fishing industry representatives, and U.S. and Canadian government agencies. The two-day meeting, is underway in Halifax, Canada, running through Nov. 17. Marine mammal scientist Heather Pettis said “seeing [the decline] is really disappointing.” She chairs this year’s meeting and leads the right whale research program at the Anderson Cabot Center. “There was a pretty significant decline following 2011 that sort of stopped in 2020, and we were starting to see this small, incremental uptick, which was fantastic. What [the latest census] says is the population is really not yet on a clear path to recovery.” North Atlantic right whales feed in the waters off Canada and the northeastern U.S. in the spring, summer and…
items.t: Drowned in fishing gear, struck by boats, North Atlantic right whales in serious trouble

items.title: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)
items.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural resources. The film ends in front of the court, as each of them, clad in white, are manhandled by police into cars and driven off to prison. The MNC5 are three men — Ly Chandaravuth, Thun Ratha, and Yim Leanghy — and two women – Phuon Keoraksmey and Long Kunthea. When they were free, they worked with local communities to educate and empower them to defend their forests, wetlands, rivers, and seas. They researched, investigated, and exposed failures to protect the environment, and they documented their activities on social media for the Cambodian people to see and comment on. They dared exercise their basic human rights by speaking out against the plunder of natural resources across the country. They urged protection for the environment, and when the authorities and their supporters ignored those calls, they dared to organize peaceful, symbolic public protests to bring attention to their demands. Ly Chandaravuth, then 24, addresses supporters before the court issued a verdict on July 2, 2024. Image courtesy of LICADHO. For daring to stand their ground, they have paid a high price. Four of them were unjustly condemned to prison for six years, while Yim Leanghy got…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Francophone leaders must support jailed Mother Nature Cambodia activists (commentary)

items.title: A ‘lost’ firefly species flashes back into view in the US
items.summary: On a June night in a meadow in the U.S. state of Delaware, Christopher Heckscher stood with his camera and waited for the fireflies to come out. Most of the flashes he saw were familiar, but a quick run of amber pulses caught his attention. “The amber color of the flash and the long rhythmic pattern did not match any other firefly I was familiar with in this region,” Heckscher, an entomologist and ecologist at Delaware State University, said in a press release. “I was confident I had found the species the moment I saw the flash pattern.” “The species” was the similar firefly (Pyractomena similis), which hadn’t been documented since 1983. Then, in spring 2026, it turned up three times, according to a new paper in the Journal of Lost Species. An illustration of the similar firefly (Pyractomena similis)by Mauricio Alvarez. An observer first spotted males flashing over a meadow in the neighboring state of Virginia on May 15 and posted the sighting to iNaturalist, a citizen science platform. A second population turned up nearby two weeks later. Heckscher’s sighting at Brandywine Creek State Park was the first record of the species in Delaware. He found it in a meadow full of shrubs, brush, and low plants. The species is known to live in open fields near water. “The habitat is not terribly common,” Heckscher said. “We think of fields and open meadows as being pretty common, but most times we’re managing them for other things, maybe livestock, or…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: A ‘lost’ firefly species flashes back into view in the US

items.title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion
items.summary:
The unfamiliar mollusk first turned up in this harvester’s haul in 2023. He asked a scientist to identify it, and together they realized they were seeing a potentially harmful, non-native species

  • Send us your climate questions for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.

Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

Continue reading...
items.t: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion

items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.summary: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.
items.t: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

items.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. Frequent power outages during the humid summer exhausted her and she was often exposed to scorching heat while traveling to see her gynecologist. At government-run Mother and Child Health Hospital in Mohammadpur, a neighborhood in western Dhaka, Hafsa gave birth to a baby boy on Nov. 7 — three weeks before a full, 40-week term. The hospital’s chief gynecologist, Nazmoon Naher, told Mongabay on Nov. 8, “We have been seeing increasing preterm births by mostly malnourished and overstressed mothers.” She could not, at the time of reporting, provide the hospital’s records of preterm deliveries. She said that mothers who gave birth earlier were required to stay in the hospital for more than three days after admission, as their babies were vulnerable to complications, including pneumonia, sepsis and gastroenteritis. Naher said that she had not specifically researched the link between extreme heat and preterm birth. Frequent power outages during the humid summer exhausted Hafsa and she was often exposed to scorching heat while traveling to see her gynecologist. Image by ASaber91 via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0). Research links heat spells and preterm births On Nov. 2, international nonprofit research group Zero Carbon Analytics released…
items.t: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests

items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds nest in the ground and incubate their eggs using environmental heat rather than body heat. “Megapodes are common across many Indonesian islands, but this is the first fossil megapode from Indonesia,” Hanneke Meijer, the study’s lead author and a paleontologist at the University Museum of Bergen, Norway, told Mongabay by email. “It shows that Indonesia also had large megapodes in the past that were similar in size to large extinct Australian megapodes.” The newly recognized species, named Megapodius rokusi, was identified from a fossilized right foot bone excavated from cave sediment layers dated to between 190,000-120,000 years ago. The researchers named the species in honor of the late Indonesian zooarchaeologist Rokus Due Awe, who played a seminal role in analyzing animal fossil remains at Liang Bua and was the first researcher to identify the hominin fossils later classified as early human species Homo floresiensis. According to the authors, M. rokusi represents the first megapode species named after an Indonesian scientist. Researchers estimated that M. rokusi weighed approximately 3.9 kilograms (8.6 pounds), making it the largest species within the genus Megapodius described to date, according to the paper. There are 12 living species of…
items.t: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia

items.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
items.summary:
Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human

The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

Continue reading...
items.t: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests

items.title: Indonesia’s domestic palm oil market carries the biggest deforestation footprint
items.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesia is the world’s biggest producer of palm oil, and the commodity is the most widely used vegetable oil across the globe. That makes all the issues associated with palm oil — from sustainability claims, to allegations of deforestation and labor abuses — the subject of close scrutiny for buyers worldwide, especially in markets with increasingly stringent environmental requirements. Yet this focus on global supply chains overlooks a major source of demand: Indonesia is the biggest consumer of its own palm oil, with more than half of total production going into the domestic market in 2024 — an all-time high driven partly by demand for biodiesel. And because the domestic market doesn’t impose strict sustainability requirements, much of the palm oil produced on deforested land is consumed within the country: For every 1,000 metric tons of crude palm oil consumed locally, 25 hectares (62 acres) of land was deforested, according to a new analysis calculating this “deforestation exposure.” It estimates that domestic consumption in 2024 was associated with 629,000 hectares (1.55 million acres) of deforested land, or two-thirds of all palm oil-related deforestation exposure; that’s nine times greater than the 71,400 hectares (176,400 acres) associated with exports to India, the largest foreign buyer of Indonesian palm oil. These figures from the analysis by Trase, a research initiative that maps commodity supply chains, reflect a 10-year historical attribution period; they don’t represent the area deforested in 2024 alone. “One of the most important issues is the…
items.t: Indonesia’s domestic palm oil market carries the biggest deforestation footprint

items.title: Rare flat-headed cat prefers elevated palms in Malaysian forest, says study
items.summary: A large camera-trap survey in a mangrove forest in southwestern Sarawak, Malaysia, has revealed new insights into the habitats and activity patterns of one of Southeast Asia’s rarest and least studied mammals: the flat-headed cat. Researchers monitored the proposed Lundu Mangrove Protected Forest across a nearly three-year survey between August 2021 and May 2024. Their cameras recorded the flat-headed cat (Prionailurus planiceps) 59 times. The small and semi-aquatic feline, native to Southeast Asia, has an elongated, flattened skull, small and set-back ears, and large, front-focused green eyes that aid in spotting aquatic prey. The cat is officially listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List. The study found most of the photos and videos of the flat-headed cat, 49 in total, were recorded in wetlands dominated by nibong palm (Oncosperma tigillarium), at slightly elevated areas located 10 to 20 meters (33 to 66 feet) above sea level. These non-tidal zones feature freshwater puddles that provide optimal foraging grounds for slippery prey like fish and amphibians. In contrast, the cats largely avoided tidally inundated swamps at or near sea level, where the cameras detected the species only once. “Out of 58 recorded detections, 48 were from Nibong, nine from Buta-buta and one from Nipah habitat,” Ahmad Ampeng, study lead author and research officer at the Forest Department Sarawak, told Mongabay. “Overall, I consider the findings important because they provide valuable ecological information about the Flat-headed Cat … a globally Endangered and elusive wild cat species.” The…
items.t: Rare flat-headed cat prefers elevated palms in Malaysian forest, says study

items.title: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic | Colin Chappell
items.summary:
Brigg, Lincolnshire: As I turn to the autumn jobs, loading crops and checking our machinery, I have to feel that next year will be better

The days are suddenly short, and the mornings have begun to turn much colder, but – strange as it may seem – I’m feeling optimistic. This happens every year around now – I look around and see well-established winter crops full of potential, hedges and edges full of food for the wildlife, and, for now, some money back in the bank, having sold some of the harvest.

The changing colours help – not only the trees but also the yellow and the browns of the soil changing back to green. Farmers have to be the ultimate gamblers, planting a crop with no idea what price we will achieve or what yield will come. We plant and hope.

Continue reading...
items.t: Country diary: A hard year on the farm, but I can’t help but feel optimistic | Colin Chappell

items.title: As butterflies sweep Sri Lanka, global study finds expanding ranges linked to climate change
items.summary: COLOMBO — For generations of Sri Lankans, the sudden appearance of thousands of yellow and white wings fluttering across the island carries a deep sense of nostalgic magic. Folklore has long framed the spectacle as a sacred pilgrimage of butterflies flying in unison toward Adam’s Peak, a conical mountain located in the island’s Central Highlands, venerated by followers of multiple faiths. In the first week of November, this familiar natural kaleidoscope returned to the country’s commercial capital Colombo, with clouds of yellow and white butterflies weaving through traffic. The phenomenon has been reported not only in Colombo but several other parts of Sri Lanka, says Lakshman Kumara, secretary of the Butterfly Conservation and Research Group of Sri Lanka (BCRG). Butterfly numbers typically peak during two main periods, October to November and February to March. While these seasonal movements occur annually, 2026’s influx has been particularly pronounced, Kumara told Mongabay. Drawing on observations from members and butterfly enthusiasts, BCRG has tracked these mass movements for several years. Kumara said the direction of the butterfly movements observed this year differ from those recorded previously, with the insects appearing to avoid the hill country, possibly because of prevailing weather conditions. A butterfly kaleidoscope. Image courtesy of Michael van Der Pooten. A 2024 study based on BCRG data documented the movement of Sri Lankan lesser albatross (Appias galene) and common albatross (Appias albina swinhoei) across Sri Lanka during March–April 2023. Based on…
items.t: As butterflies sweep Sri Lanka, global study finds expanding ranges linked to climate change

items.title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?
items.summary:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS

Continue reading...
items.t: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?

items.title: Indiana Jones at the fish market: David Ebert on a life spent searching for ‘lost sharks’
items.summary: If there’s an Indiana Jones of the shark world, David Ebert is it. Known as the “Lost Shark Guy,” the Californian marine biologist has spent his career traveling the globe in search of little- or unknown species of sharks and their cousins, the rays and chimaeras. It often begins with a photograph or a museum specimen of a shark not seen live in decades. Ebert will hit the road to try to confirm if the animal is still out there. He often ends up at pungent-smelling fish markets or remote landing sites, “up to my elbows in shark guts.” The creatures he’s found have often been completely new to science. Over the past 40 years, Ebert has described and named 56 species, from the big-nosed lanternshark (Etmopterus bulbosus) and the Arabian black electric ray (Tetronarce ramanamurthyi), to Lana’s sawshark (Pristiophorus lanae), named for his niece as a present for her college graduation. He has another half-dozen species in the pipeline. Top: Big-nosed lanternshark Ebert named in August 2026. It’s a contender for the world’s smallest shark, with a maximum known length of 21 centimeters, or about 8 inches. Bottom left: Arabian black electric ray. Bottom right: Lana’s sawshark. Images courtesy of David Ebert. “There’s nothing cooler than finding some sharks that are rare or a new species,” Ebert tells Mongabay. “You forget everything that stinks or smells around you when you start seeing some really cool sharks and rays like that.” Ebert is a fierce advocate for lesser-known sharks and rays,…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Indiana Jones at the fish market: David Ebert on a life spent searching for ‘lost sharks’

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.summary: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.
items.t: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

items.title: Chickens are great characters, not cowards | Letters
items.summary:
Jo Barlow kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, brave and funny

Whoever deemed chickens synonymous with cowardice obviously didn’t tell my 14-year‑old bantam who took on a hungry Harris hawk and won (Chickens are synonymous with cowardice. Is it time to stick up for our feathered friends?, 11 November).

I kept chickens for more than 15 years and found them to be intelligent, unique characters who could be brave, funny, naughty, loving and kind in equal measure.

items.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
items.summary:
Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations

Your article (Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century.

There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes.

items.t: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters

items.title: Return of the wild oyster: conservationists bring shellfish back from local extinction off Scottish coast
items.summary:
Scientists succeed in breeding wild oysters in Dornoch Firth, near Inverness, from where they disappeared more than 100 years ago

The baby oysters, with their rough cream-coloured shells and ragged edges, are about the size of a 50 pence piece. But off the north-east coast of Scotland, they are proof of a breakthrough in marine conservation.

For the first time in the UK, scientists have succeeded in breeding wild oysters at a site where they had been locally extinct for more than a century, in the Dornoch Firth north of Inverness.

Continue reading...
items.t: Return of the wild oyster: conservationists bring shellfish back from local extinction off Scottish coast

items.title: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
items.summary: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.
items.t: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

items.title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
items.summary: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.
items.t: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

items.title: Targeted by al-Shabaab for defending Kenya’s ecosystems: Foundation founder gets award
items.summary: Conservation is rarely conflict-free. On Kenya’s northern coastline, in Lamu and Tana River counties — a biodiversity hotspot where the nation’s longest river meets the Indian Ocean — the work of protecting marine and terrestrial habitats often takes a willingness to challenge industrial fishing and extractive industries. For Raabia Hawa, defending nature against these activities has meant operating in areas largely neglected by official conservation bodies. A former broadcast journalist and Montessori teacher turned environmental defender, Hawa founded the Ulinzi Africa Foundation (“Ulinzi” means the defenders in Swahili) in 2014 to provide frontline ranger patrols against elephant poaching and wildlife crime. Her work has since expanded beyond anti-poaching to combat illegal industrial bottom-trawling and empower local communities resisting extractive mining concessions. Operating near the Somali border comes with high political insecurity. Hawa’s vocal stance against environmental destruction has come at a personal risk, including death threats and being designated a target by the militant group al-Shabaab. Despite these perils, Ulinzi has continued to operate on a shoestring, powered by volunteer family support. In London to receive the 2026 Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa — which provides Ulinzi with three years of critical funding — Hawa spoke with Mongabay about the realities of countering industrial fishing and mobilizing rural women against mining giants, highlighting the disconnect between global biodiversity targets and the daily battles frontline nature…
items.t: Targeted by al-Shabaab for defending Kenya’s ecosystems: Foundation founder gets award

items.title: Lioness Attacks And Ends The Life Of A 19YO After Being Let Out Of Its Cage For A TikTok Video
items.summary:
A TikTok video captured at a private wildlife farm in Lahore, Pakistan, ended in tragedy after a lioness attacked and slayed a 19-year-old farm worker. 

The young man, identified in reports as Talha, was called over to film content with the big cat after a TikToker arrived at the property. 

However, the animal allegedly became uncontrollable after being let out of its cage. 

The teenager was rushed to a private hospital but later passed away from his injuries . 

Police have since arrested the farm’s owner and the content creator as they investigate what happened. 

The incident has also sparked anger online, with one person reminding others that “lions aren’t stage props.” 

A 19-year-old farm worker lost his life after a lioness was let out for a TikTok video 

Sefa Demirtaş/Pexels (not the real image) 

The fatal incident took place at around 5 p.m. on November 11 at a private wildlife farm in Kahna, Lahore. 

According to reports, the 19-year-old employee was working at the property when TikToker Nouman Hassan arrived to film a video with the lioness. 

Hassan, who reportedly has around 928,000 followers on TikTok and 2.5 million on Instagram, is known for posting videos featuring big cats. 

According to a police complaint cited by the BBC , Hassan allegedly asked the farm worker to join him for the video. He then took the lioness out of its cage and began filming. 

Lahore Police 

However, the situation quickly turned dangerous when the animal reportedly became erratic and attacked the teenager. Talha suffered critical injuries and was taken to a…
items.t: Lioness Attacks And Ends The Life Of A 19YO After Being Let Out Of Its Cage For A TikTok Video

items.title: Spicy ping-pong balls and flaming dung keep elephants at bay in Zimbabwe
items.summary: On the front line of the human-elephant conflict, coming up with non-lethal methods of protecting crops means getting creative. In one village in Zimbabwe, a multilayered approach is taken – first a fence covered in chili infused rags and chili powder traps, if that fails elephant dung covered in chili oil is set alight, finally as a last resort a makeshift bazooka (powered by a deodorant) fires chili-oil filled ping-pong balls at persistent elephants. The last elephant who took a pingpong ball to the face did not return to the village for over a year.This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Spicy ping-pong balls and flaming dung keep elephants at bay in Zimbabwe

items.title: Bristol aims to become UK’s first ‘wetland city’ and reduce flood risk
items.summary:
Five-year project will create wildlife corridors by building wetlands and increase access to green and blue spaces

Bristol could become home to the UK’s first “wetland city” thanks to a charity’s efforts to create vast wildlife corridors that will reduce flood risk and give people more access to green and blue spaces.

The Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (WWT) said the five-year initiative would include more than 200 projects to restore and create wetlands across the city. These will range from small household rainwater ponds and street-level rain gardens to restoring river habitats, reconnecting rivers with their floodplains, and creating new wetlands.

Continue reading...
items.t: Bristol aims to become UK’s first ‘wetland city’ and reduce flood risk

items.title: ‘An environmental and welfare disaster’: British salmon loses its organic status
items.summary:
This week the Soil Association withdrew certification from organic salmon after 20 years. What went wrong?

The first haul of farmed salmon in Britain was a relatively modest 14 tonnes, produced off the west coast of Scotland near Fort William in 1971.

For Unilever, the vast multinational that pioneered salmon farming, it was a triumph after years of experimenting with how to cage fish, battle against diseases and cope with the wild weather. Unilever had spotted in the 1960s that farming salmon, which until then was caught wild and remained a relative luxury, would create a mass market, lower costs and provide steady profits. By 1976, it had expanded into three Scottish sites producing 116 tonnes of fish each year.

items.t: ‘An environmental and welfare disaster’: British salmon loses its organic status

items.title: South African court dismisses appeal over planned coal-fired power plants
items.summary: The South African Supreme Court of Appeal recently dismissed the government’s appeal against a ruling that struck down plans for 1,500 megawatts of new coal-fired power. The so-called #CancelCoal case was brought by a coalition of environmental NGOs that argued the new planned coal capacity violates children’s constitutional rights to a healthy environment. Already, air pollution from coal-fired power plants kills more than 2,200 South Africans each year and “causes thousands of cases of bronchitis and asthma,” according to a statement from the Centre for Environmental Rights. The Minister of Electricity and Energy argued that additional coal capacity is necessary for energy security. A previous High Court judgment ruled against the plan “on the basis that it violates the right to an environment not harmful to health and well-being,” per the statement. “The High Court further found that government’s arguments about grid stability offered by coal, was not sufficient justification for the violation of constitutional rights,” said Michelle Sithole in an email to Mongabay. Sithole is senior associate in the pollution and climate change program at the Centre for Environmental Rights, the group that represented the plaintiffs in the court case. The Minister appealed the High Court decision. The recent Court of Appeal’s decision dismissed the Minister’s appeal, meaning the previous High Court decision stands. “While this does not mean a definitive end to the development of new coal-fired power as part of the energy security policy, it does mean that government has a higher…
items.t: South African court dismisses appeal over planned coal-fired power plants

items.title: Honduras declares ‘environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
items.summary: Deforestation, organized crime and the expansion of cattle ranching have led the government in Honduras to announce an “environmental emergency” in the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, the largest protected area in the country. The 36-month emergency, issued as a presidential decree on Nov. 10, will devote 1.5 billion Honduran lempiras (more than $55 million) over the next three years to halt “environmental deterioration,” according to an official statement. “The initiative represents a commitment by the government to move from addressing threats to sustained intervention, with defined resources and institutional responsibilities,” presidential legal advisor Roberto Zacapa said in the statement. The more than 832,000-hectare (2 million-acre) reserve stretches across the departments of Gracias a Dios, Colón and Olancho, and includes numerous Indigenous Miskito, Pech and Garífuna communities. In 1982, a section of it was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The reserve’s remote location along the Nicaraguan border has made it vulnerable to deforestation, drug trafficking, cattle ranching, gold mining, wildlife trafficking, roadbuilding and other illegal activities. At least 6,691 hectares (16,533 acres) of forest were cut down between 2023 and 2025, according to the Forest Conservation Institute (ICF), the agency managing the country’s forests. Since 2011, the reserve has been on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage in Danger, a list of sites facing serious threats to their environmental or cultural heritage. “It’s like the wild west, where there’s no law and people come in…
items.t: Honduras declares ‘environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve

items.title: Monty Don was the best teacher and presenter imaginable | Letters
items.summary:
Saul Abbott says his pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him, Jane Bates values Gardeners’ World immeasurably, while Joe Mackenzie shares a poignant memory

I started my professional gardening career in 2004, a year after Monty started presenting Gardeners’ World (‘It’s the final goodbye’: Monty Don bows out with a blissful last Gardeners’ World, 6 November).

To say this great man taught me much of what I have learned since is a gross understatement. Not just about the principles and practices of gardening itself, but the understanding in a greater sense of what a garden is, what it gives to us both in bounty, tangibly, and nourishment of something far greater, internally.

items.title: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US
items.summary: A record number of wildfires burned more than 14,062 square miles in the U.S. this year, leaving behind charred trees and scorched vegetation. But less-obvious are the impacts they had on the streams and rivers that provide drinking water to urban and rural communities across the country. After a wildfire burns a watershed, rain will carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities. Utilities must turn off the intake to keep the sediment-filled water from contaminating their systems and switch to another source, if it’s available. New studies found that wildfires can contaminate water for up to 15 years. These findings are especially concerning as climate change has led to an increase in the number and size of wildfires in the U.S. By Martha Bellisele, Associated Press Banner image: A helicopter drops water on the Grizzly Creek Fire on the east end of Glenwood Canyon, Aug. 17, 2020 near Glenwood Springs, Colo. Image courtesy of Helen H. Richardson/The Denver Post via Associated PressThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US

items.title: There’s no substitute for getting out of the classroom and into nature (analysis)
items.summary: Leading a group of ecology students down a trail through the forest behind Merrimack College, in North Andover, Massachusetts, U.S., where I teach biology part-time as an adjunct professor, I spot a garter snake. As it rapidly starts crawling away, I grab the snake by its tail. Excited students gather round to check out the foot-long striped serpent, while taking photos with their cell phones. I tell them a bit about garter snakes and ask if anyone wants to hold it. “I do!” one of the students says. I gently hand her the snake. “That’s really cool. I’ve never held a snake before,” she says, before handing it to another eager student. Then we turn the snake loose and continue on our way. Merrimack College biology students with a garter snake found during an ecology lab on campus, North Andover, MA, September 2025. Image courtesy of Don Lyman. Since I began at Merrimack in 1997, I’ve taught mainly ecology labs. Most of the ecology lab sessions are outdoors, so they’re like weekly field trips. They give students the opportunity to step outside of laboratories and classrooms and interact with nature. Field courses provide the same opportunity for teachers. When I head off into the woods with students in tow, I’m in my element. Whether I’m diving into the bushes and scrambling on my hands and knees to catch a snake or a frog to show the class, pointing out a hawk circling overhead, or teaching students how to identify various…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: There’s no substitute for getting out of the classroom and into nature (analysis)

items.title: Mongabay shark meat investigation shortlisted for two journalism awards in Brazil
items.summary: A Mongabay investigation that revealed large-scale government purchases of shark meat for schools, hospitals, prisons and other public institutions in Brazil has been named as a finalist for two Brazilian journalism awards               . Published in 2025 in collaboration with the Pulitzer Center, the investigation tracked 1,012 public procurements issued since 2004 to purchase more than 5,400 metric tons of shark meat, worth at least 112 million reais ($20.1 million). The findings sparked environmental and public health concerns. Sharks, some of them endangered, accumulate heavy metals such as mercury and arsenic in their tissues. High levels of these contaminants can pose health risks, particularly for children. Mongabay’s reporting is one of three finalists for the Cláudio Weber Abramo Data Journalism Award in the investigation category, which recognizes “work of high social impact that applies data analysis to shed light on topics of public interest.” The series is also one of 25 finalists for the Mosca Award, which honors investigative reporting and projects focused on transparency, access to public information and open data. Senior editor Philip Jacobson and investigative reporters Karla Mendes and Fernanda Wenzel reported the series for Mongabay, working with Kuang Keng Kuek Ser, then data editor at the Pulitzer Center. The investigation has had widespread impact, prompting a request for a public hearing in Brazil’s lower house of Congress and stirring debate in the fishing industry over the risks of eating shark meat. Shark meat was banned in 1,200 schools run by…
items.t: Mongabay shark meat investigation shortlisted for two journalism awards in Brazil

items.title: ‘Incredibly unusual’ bird migrating from Siberia found in Cumbria – killed by cat

Siberian rubythroat was thousands of miles off course from its route to winter in south or south-east Asia

A bird that flies south from its breeding grounds in Siberia to winter in south and south-east Asia has been found thousands of miles off course in Cumbria. Regrettably, it was found by a cat.

Chris Hind, Cumbria’s county recorder for birds, said it was “extraordinary” that a Siberian rubythroat was found on his patch, albeit dead. There have been only 17 recorded instances of the bird in the UK, 15 of those in the northern Scottish isles.

items.title: A super El Niño brings startling changes for marine life on California coast: ‘like nothing we’ve ever seen’

Water temperatures are climbing the charts, high tides are swallowing the shoreline and vital parts of the food web that feed ocean diversity are disappearing

On a picturesque autumn afternoon last week, the beaches of California’s Monterey Bay were teeming with life and death.

A cadre of shorebirds charged and retreated in a synchronized dance with the raging surf. Nearby, the receding tides had deposited lifeless bundles of feathers and bone, tangled in piles of glistening kelp. Swollen sea lion carcasses, their teeth bared in a quiet grimace, dotted the sand as beach picnickers and dog walkers enjoyed the warm, cloudless day.

items.title: This Animal Clinic Discovered Four Kittens Abandoned Inside A Box Outside Their Office And Helped Them Get Adopted
items.summary:
Finding a box of potato chips outside your workplace usually just means a quick trip to the garbage disposal. But when staff at the Blue Cross animal hospital in Hammersmith, London, arrived for work one morning, they discovered something rather unexpected inside such a box: four tiny kittens who had been abandoned and left to fend for themselves.

Fortunately, the little ones had ended up in the right place. The veterinary team quickly took them in, checked their health, and made sure they received the care they needed. And although their lives had gotten off to a rather unfortunate start, things were about to take a much happier turn. You might remember Blue Cross from our recent story about Bowie, the pony who grew up surrounded by cows. The UK animal welfare charity helps thousands of animals through its veterinary services, rescue efforts, and rehoming centers, giving pets in difficult circumstances another chance at a happy life.

Scroll down to see how the kittens are doing now and read the rest of the story.

The charity believes the ongoing cost-of-living crisis may be contributing, with some owners avoiding neutering their pets because of veterinary expenses. There are also concerns about people breeding cats to sell their kittens, only to struggle to find buyers and ultimately surrender or abandon the animals. “We’re so happy we managed to help these kittens into loving homes so quickly, and in time for Christmas,” Amanda Rumball, Veterinary Welfare Officer at Blue Cross, shared.

“We are urging anyone who is struggling to care for any…

items.title: Country diary: Why did some trees fall in the storms and others not? It could be spalting | Kate Blincoe
items.summary:
Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: The woodland floor is littered with sycamore and ash, some revealing a pattern that runs through trunks like words in a stick of rock

An ash tree swayed, audibly groaning, a split in the trunk opening and closing like a mouth. Suffering from ash dieback, it seemed it could topple at any second here in the quiet of the woodland. A few weeks ago, Dad set the trail camera on it, to capture the moment of fall. Since then, two storms have churned through Norfolk – treating us gently compared with elsewhere, but nevertheless leaving casualties in their wake.

Fallen trunks now crisscross the woodland floor: sycamores, several ashes, an oak. But not the ash that had seemed so vulnerable. Why does one tree survive but another fall? I look closely at one of the ashes that succumbed to the winds, with its headless trunk jutting skyward, spiked and bare.

Continue reading...
items.t: Country diary: Why did some trees fall in the storms and others not? It could be spalting | Kate Blincoe

items.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
items.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

items.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
items.summary: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.
items.t: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

items.title: First guidelines on attempts to manipulate the ocean put spotlight on geoengineering industry
items.summary:
Proponents argue ocean carbon removal is necessary to counteract the effects of the climate crisis but critics say more research is needed

A cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon.

“This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies.

items.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.
